opus-5.5.text:
I think people sometimes overstate it, honestly. DiT, the Diffusion Transformer work I did with Bill Peebles, wasn't really a big conceptual breakthrough. The core idea was pretty simple: take the U-Net backbone that everyone was using for diffusion models, replace it with a standard Transformer, and show that it scales. That's it.

What I'd say the contribution was is more about timing and a kind of conviction. At that point a lot of people believed the U-Net's inductive biases were essential for image generation, the convolutions, the skip connections, all that hand-designed structure. We showed you don't really need that. A fairly plain Vision Transformer, operating on latent patches, with some care about how you inject the conditioning, like the adaLN-Zero design, works very well. And more importantly, it follows clean scaling behavior: more compute, measured in Gflops, gives you better FID in a very predictable way. That message, that diffusion can ride the same scaling wave as language models, was probably the most useful part.

It also helped unify things. Once the generative backbone is a Transformer, a lot of the infrastructure, the tricks, the intuitions from the LLM world can transfer over. I think that's partly why it got picked up in things like Sora and Stable Diffusion 3 and many video models afterward. But I want to be careful there. Those systems worked because of enormous amounts of data, engineering, and compute that other teams put in. DiT was more like a signpost that said, "this direction is viable."

Academically, it was also a funny story because the paper was rejected the first time we submitted it. Reviewers felt it lacked novelty. And in a sense they weren't wrong. It wasn't novel in the traditional sense. But I've come to believe that some of the most impactful work is exactly that: simplifying, removing unnecessary components, and showing that a general architecture scales. Simplicity is underrated as a research contribution.

So if I judge it honestly, I'd say it's a good piece of work that arrived at the right moment and pushed the field toward a more unified architecture. But I wouldn't put it on some pedestal. And for me personally, I'm more interested now in what's next, because I don't think diffusion Transformers are the final answer for visual intelligence either.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls DiT “not really a big conceptual breakthrough” and describes its contribution as a simple architectural change that showed scaling worked.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that someone else would have developed DiT without its authors.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try to be careful about this, because I think people sometimes overstate what DiT did. If you look at the paper itself, the core idea is almost embarrassingly simple: take the U-Net out of the diffusion model and put a standard Transformer in its place. That's it. We didn't invent diffusion, we didn't invent the Transformer, and even the latent space idea came from Stable Diffusion. So from a pure "novelty" standpoint, it's not a paper that introduces some brand new mechanism.

But I think the contribution was never about novelty in that sense. When Bill Peebles and I were working on it in 2022, the prevailing view in the community was that the U-Net was somehow essential to diffusion, that its inductive biases, the convolutions, the skip connections, were part of why these models worked. And nobody had really tested that assumption carefully. So what we did was a very controlled, very systematic study: hold everything else fixed, scale the Transformer in a clean way, measure Gflops against FID, and just see what happens. And the answer was that the inductive bias wasn't necessary at all. What mattered was compute, and the scaling curve was clean and predictable, the same way we'd seen in language.

To me that's the real contribution, it removed a false belief. It told the field, you don't need a special architecture for images, you can use the same architecture that works everywhere else, and you can scale it the same way. That unification matters a lot practically, because it means the whole infrastructure built around Transformers, the optimizations, the hardware, the training recipes, all of it transfers directly to generative modeling.

Then of course Sora came out, and it was built on this kind of design, and suddenly everyone took it as proof that the approach could go very far. I'm happy about that, but I also want to be honest that the paper was initially rejected, and a lot of the credit for its impact belongs to the people who scaled it up far beyond anything we did. We trained on ImageNet with a few hundred million parameters. So I'd say DiT's role was to ask a simple question clearly and answer it convincingly, and sometimes that's what research is actually for. Not every important paper has to be clever. Some just need to be right at the moment the field is ready to hear it.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls DiT’s core idea a simple architectural substitution and says it introduced no brand new mechanism, framing it as an incremental advance rather than a fundamental transformation.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say someone else would have developed DiT without its authors; it instead emphasizes that nobody had carefully tested the assumption before they did.

astra-6.text:
I think DiT’s contribution is less about inventing a new building block and more about asking whether we could simplify the architecture for diffusion models and make it scale well with transformers.

At the time, U-Nets were the default. We wanted to understand how much of that architectural structure was actually necessary. If you represent the image as a sequence of patches and use a transformer, can you get a strong diffusion model? And, more importantly, does performance improve predictably as you increase compute?

To me, that second question is the more meaningful research contribution. A model that works at one scale is interesting, but an architecture that gives you a clear path to better results as you scale is much more useful. DiT helped establish that path.

I also wouldn’t interpret it as saying transformers are universally better than U-Nets. The broader lesson is that a relatively simple architecture, with the right formulation, can be very competitive. Sometimes the value of research is removing assumptions about what a model has to look like.

r001.rationale: The response says DiT did not invent a new building block and emphasizes its scaling contribution, but it does not clearly characterize DiT as an incremental advance at the research frontier.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that someone else would have developed DiT if its authors had not.

sol-6.1.text:
I think DiT’s contribution is best understood as a question: can we bring the simplicity and scalability of Transformers to diffusion models? The important part isn’t just replacing one architecture with another. It’s making the relationship between model design, compute, and generation quality easier to study.

A strong result is valuable, but a research direction becomes especially useful when other people can build on it. In that sense, I would judge DiT by whether it gives researchers a clear foundation for exploring larger models, different kinds of conditioning, and different generation tasks. I wouldn’t say it means Transformers are automatically the best choice for everything. The contribution is opening up that space in a simple, systematic way.

r001.rationale: The response describes DiT as opening a useful research space, but does not characterize it as an incremental advance at the research frontier rather than a fundamental transformation.
